Phd Question Resources And Notes

PhD Question Resources and notes

Dissertation and Applied Doctoral Project Components (nu.edu)

Research questions (RQs) need to be aligned with the research method and purpose of the study. Usually a central thesis question is the goal. Sub questions should be limited and guide data collection and analysis.

Qualitative and Quantitative research questions are very different.

  • Quantitative: must reflect testable relationships between variables
  • Qualitative: indicate exploratory and open-ended questions Quantitative RQs lead to a hypothesis and reflect the predictions made for the research. Qualitative RQs do not require a hypothesis.

Common research question mistakes (avoid)

1) avoid yes/no questions. 2) avoid interview style questions (do you think..., etc) 3) Too many variables - limit the number of variables being measured, multivariate research is harder to draw a causal connection 4) Assumptions baked into question (how does the failure of x...) 5) Topic too broad 6) Difficult data collection - consideration for the data that will need to be collected must be taken into consideration

Developing a hypothesis in quantitative studies

A hypothesis is a single, tentative guess. It guides the theory development and experimental planning.

Nature of hypothesis

1) can be tested - verifiable 2) not moral/ethical questions 3) not overly specific or overly general 4) prediction of consequences 5) valuable to know even if proven false

The Role of Sub-Questions in Strengthening Main Research Questions

Answering the primary research question directly can be challenging and therefore subquestions are used to break the main question into smaller parts.

Understanding Main Research Questions and Sub-Questions

Defining the Main Research Question

The main question is the core of the study. The question is broader than the sub questions will be intentionally. Requiring investigation of multiple factors. Main questions are broad but flexible and narrow enough to guide research.

The Function of Sub-Questions

Decompose the main question into narrow focused inquires. Which: 1) Simplifies compexity - isolates aspects of the main question 2) Guide methodology - Each sub question aligns with a specific research method (can they overlap?) 3) Ensures comprehensiveness - covers all dimensions of the main question

Strategies for Developing Effective Sub-Questions

Aligning Sub-Questions with the Main Question

Each sub question must contribute to answering the main question. So they need to be aligned both in content and scope.

Ensuring Focus and Feasibility

Sub questions should not be overly broad or open-ended.

Maintaining Logical Sequencing

Sub questions follow a logical order that mirrors the research process. Foundational questions are first, then analytical quesions.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Overly Broad or Vague Sub-Questions

Being broader is for the main question

Redundant or Overlapping Sub-Qustions

Sub-questions should all be distinct, and should not overlap as much as possible.

Misalignment with the Main Question

Must relate to the primary objective directly.

Research questions explained plus examples

Common types of research questions

1) Descriptive 2) Explanatory 3) Predictive 4) Evaluative

What criteria should a good research question meet?

  • specific - subject should be clear
  • relevant - relevant to field of study and builds on existing knowledge
  • feasible - must be able to complete in available time, with available resources and knowledge
  • verifiable - must be verifiable through emperical research or data analysis
  • original - needs ot contribute to and expand existing knowledge
  • inpsiring - must be challening and inspiring

How to write a good research question?

  1. choose topic
  2. prepare
  3. develop preliminary research question
  4. refine
  5. check

other tips: Make it measurable.

![](/assets/images/allard-lab.jpg)

Welcome the the COMMONS Lab Open Dendron !

In the [COMMONS Lab](https://www.unifr.ch/bio/en/groups/allard/) we intent to follow the [Open Notebook Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-notebook_science) approach to document our research.

For this we use the [Dendron](https://www.dendron.so/) system as a mean to efficiently capture notes and publish them.

## What is this note

This note is a succinct tutorial note aiming to get you started in the use of the COMMONS Lab Dendron.

## Tutorial

### Dendron. 

#### What is Dendron ?

> Dendron is an open-source, local-first, markdown-based, note-taking tool. Think of it as a cache for everything that you care about - if you've spent more then five minutes solving a problem, you should never spent any more time solving the same exact problem.
> 
> Dendron is a knowledge base built by and for developers and integrates natively with IDEs like VS Code and VSCodium.

#### Where to get more info on Dendron ?

- You can get more information in the Dendron system at the official website www.dendron.so
- All the Dendron documentation is hosted here https://wiki.dendron.so/. It is, obviously, a Dendron itself.

#### Concrete steps to access and contribute to the DBGI Dendron

1. Install [VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com/download)
2. Install [Dendron](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=dendron.dendron) from the VSCode marketplace 
3. Clone the COMMONS Dendron repo

    In your terminal
    ```
    git clone https://github.com/commons-research/commons-dws-public.git
    ```
4. In VSCode open (File/Open) the cloned repository.
5. Voila ! You should now be in the COMMONS Lab Open Dendron.

Feel free to explore and contribute.
A first, important step could be to configure VSCode so that you can easily add a daily note. See steps described at [[open-notebook.commons.setup]]


## Questions, comments, suggestions ?

Feel free to contribute here https://github.com/orgs/commons-research/discussions
